chapter_theme: The eagerness for union overrides every plan to sulk. She can't see his faults once he is in view, and sets out to quarrel but her heart betrays her. The chapter's most quoted verse states why: love is more delicate than a flower, and few catch its moment.
structure_note: Parimelazhagar gives 1281-1287 to the woman speaking to her friend, 1288 to the friend speaking to the man, and 1289-1290 to the man, faced with a sulk that won't end. Manakkudavar gives 1288 and 1289 to the woman.

1281.reading: The woman says that being intoxicated at a thought and delighted at a look belong not to liquor but to love.
1281.nuance: Parimelazhagar's setting is pointed: the friend teases her about why she isn't angry at a man planning to leave. So the famous line is an excuse. He also distinguishes the words: களித்தல், with awareness intact, and மகிழ்தல், with awareness lost.

1282.reading: The woman says that when love fills to the size of a palmyra tree, there should be no sulking, not even the size of a millet seed.
1282.nuance: The huge and tiny are the proverbial measures. Parimelazhagar says she seems to be giving others good advice, and is in fact describing her own eagerness. Manakkudavar has her say this to her own heart, which is thinking of sulking.

1283.reading: The woman says that though he disregards her and does only what pleases him, her eyes won't rest without seeing him.
1283.nuance: It's a clear admission, with no self-deception. He is at fault, she knows it, and the eyes don't care. Pope's prose wrongly makes the eyes the ones who disregard her; the commentators and his couplet agree it is the man.

1284.reading: The woman tells her friend that she went there to sulk, but her heart forgot that and went there to unite.
1284.nuance: The same verb, சென்றேன் and சென்றது, is used for both: she and her heart set out together and went to different places. Parimelazhagar's word for this is அறைபோக, treason in a military sense.

1285.reading: The woman says that, as the eye can't see the stick that lines it at the moment of lining, she doesn't see her husband's fault when she sees him.
1285.nuance: A wonderfully precise image: the object is at its closest and most intimate exactly when it can't be seen. Parimelazhagar notes that the eye knows the stick well enough at other times, and so she too knows his faults.

1286.reading: The woman says that when she sees him she doesn't see his faults, and when she doesn't see him she sees nothing but his faults.
1286.nuance: A perfectly symmetrical verse about what presence does to judgement. As with the previous verse, this isn't presented as an illusion that she can see through and correct; it's just how it is. Sight is what removes her power to judge him.

1287.reading: The woman asks what use it is to sulk, knowing it will fail, like those who jump into a stream knowing it will carry them off.
1287.nuance: Parimelazhagar registers a strain in the syntax, and offers an alternate shape: 'I learned by trying once that sulking fails; I won't do it again'. Pope's couplet is rather different in having a rescue. The swimmer who knows she'll be swept away jumps in anyway, and the verse doesn't deny that this might be the fun of it.

1288.reading: Thief, your chest is to us as liquor is to those who drink it, though it does them shameful harm; the speaker is the friend for Parimelazhagar and the woman for Manakkudavar.

positions.position: The friend tells the man that she has seen the woman's eagerness, and uses 'us' for them both.
positions.quote: தலைமகள் புணர்ச்சி? விதுப்பு அறிந்த தோழி, தலைமகற்குச் சொல்லியது.

positions.position: The woman speaks to the man herself, having let go of the wish to sulk.
positions.quote: இது புலவிக்குறிப்பு நீங்கின தலை மகள் தலைமகற்குச் சொல்லியது

1289.reading: Love is softer than a flower, and few attain its moment; the speaker is the man for Parimelazhagar and the woman, to her heart, for Manakkudavar.
1289.nuance: The famous line has a practical use. Parimelazhagar lists what makes this moment rare: two people need to share intent, desire, enjoyment and pleasure at one time, in a fit place, moment and setting. He has the man saying this to end her sulk, so the maxim is also a plea.

positions.position: The man speaks during a sulk that won't yield to his pleading, in order to end it.
The woman, seeing that he desires union, tells her own heart that this isn't the moment to sulk.
positions.quote: இப்பொழுது ஊடுவையாயின், இக்காமஞ் செவ்விதப்பு மென்று புணர்ச்சி வேட்கையால் தலைமகள் நெஞ்சோடு கூறியது.

1290.reading: The man recalls that she sulked with her eyes alone and then, more eager than he for the embrace, was undone.
1290.nuance: Parimelazhagar gives this an edge: spoken during her present sulk, it means 'the woman who gave up so quickly was not this one'. Manakkudavar has him simply observing her now. A rare moment of him looking back on her eagerness, and one that might flatter him.

links.note: 104 says that those who know value a favour the size of a millet seed as if it were a palmyra. 1282 uses the same pair for love and sulking. The scale of ethical gratitude is used for measuring love's excess, and this time the small thing is to be removed altogether.

Both state that he doesn't truly cherish her (பேணாது) and that the eyes can't rest without seeing him (காணாது அமை-). In 1178 this is a complaint on her eyes' folly, and in 1283 it's her reason for not quarrelling. The same fact has moved from grief to an explanation.

In 1127 she won't line her eyes because he's within them and would be hidden. In 1285 the stick is what the eye can't see. In the absence, kohl was an obstacle. In his presence, he himself is like the stick, too close to be seen.

90 says that a guest wilts at a cold look as an anicham flower wilts when smelled. 1289 makes love softer still than a flower. In both, what is finest about a relationship fails at a slight change in the other person's face.

1259 tells it in her voice: I went to sulk, my heart gave way. 1290 tells it in his: she sulked with her eyes and came faster than I did. Each tells the other's defeat as a private pleasure, though for her it's defeat, and for him it's a fond memory.

source_issues: 1283: Pope's prose makes the eyes disregard the speaker, which conflicts with his couplet and with the commentators.
1288: Parimelazhagar's headnote has a stray question mark, புணர்ச்சி? விதுப்பு.
